listenAndRepeat.scenarioTitle: Front Desk Orientation at the Clinic
listenAndRepeat.scenarioDescription: You are about to hear a clinic front-desk coordinator walk a new trainee through the front desk before their first solo shift. Listen to each sentence the coordinator says and repeat what you hear. Repeat only once.

image.prompt:
FLAT VECTOR INFOGRAPHIC ILLUSTRATION, one square image.

VIEW: elevated three-quarter "illustrated map" view of the whole location at once, quasi-isometric — the ground/floor is drawn as flattened foreshortened shapes seen from above at an angle, while furniture, equipment and people are drawn in near-side elevation. The entire setting is visible in one frame, like a hand-drawn guide map of the place.

COLOR — this is the most important rule. The environment is STRICTLY GRAYSCALE / ACHROMATIC: near-white background (#FAFAFA), pale gray surfaces (#E6E6E6), mid grays (#D2D2D2, #C8C8C8), darker gray for the nearest foreground (#A0A0A0), and dark gray to near-black line work (#505050). NO color anywhere in the environment — no blue, no green, no brown floors, no colored walls. This applies without exception to things that are normally colored: WATER AND SWIMMING POOLS ARE GRAY, NOT BLUE OR CYAN; glass is gray; plants, trees and grass are gray, not green; sky is near-white.

SPOT COLOR: exactly one accent hue, a soft muted teal (#00A082), used ONLY as a rounded organic highlight blob sitting behind and hugging the silhouette of each KEY OBJECT listed below, making those objects pop out of the gray scene. The key objects themselves may be muted golden-tan (#FABE50) or rust brown (#965A32). Nothing else in the picture carries any hue.

LINE: crisp, clean, uniform thin line weight throughout, like a printed vector diagram rather than a pencil sketch. Every surface is a COMPLETELY FLAT FILL of one single solid tone — NO gradients, NO soft shading, NO drop shadows, NO ambient occlusion, NO texture, NO hatching, NO photorealism, NO 3D rendering. Depth is conveyed only by stacking flat bands of different gray tones.

PEOPLE: a few small, simple, FACELESS grayscale figures in candid poses — plain oval heads with no facial features at all, no skin tone, no clothing color.

FRAMING: the illustration sits inside a thin black rectangular border with a generous clean margin. Uncluttered and airy, not crowded.

ABSOLUTELY NO TEXT: no letters, no words, no numbers, no labels, no captions, no signage text, no logos, no watermarks, no arrows. Any sign must be blank or a wordless pictogram only.

SCENE TO ILLUSTRATE: Front Desk Orientation at the Clinic. You are about to hear a clinic front-desk coordinator walk a new trainee through the front desk before their first solo shift. Listen to each sentence the coordinator says and repeat what you hear. Repeat only once.

Draw the location as a single connected scene. These are the KEY OBJECTS and areas that must be clearly visible and individually recognizable, each marked with the teal highlight blob:
- The sign-in sheet stays stacked beside the appointment binder.
- New trainees and returning patients both use this counter.
- Check the blood pressure cuff before every single patient visit.
- You'll greet each patient, and you'll confirm their appointment time.
- After you finish each visit, restock the closet with bandages and gauze.
- Keep the exam room door closed between patients so visits stay private.
- The supply closet, restocked each morning, keeps every station ready for patients.

Depict the physical places and things named above (the counter, the doors, the rooms, the equipment) as recognizable drawn objects in their spatial relationship to each other. Do not write any of these words in the image — show them as pictures only.

interview.scenarioTitle: A Quick Call About Your Part-Time Job
interview.intro: You are about to take part in a short phone interview about your part-time job. A researcher studying workplace routines will ask you four questions. You will have no time to prepare, so just answer as completely as you can within the time given.

questions.question: Thank you for speaking with me today. To start, could you tell me what kind of part-time job you currently have, and about how many hours a typical shift lasts?
Great. Now think of one shift that really stood out to you, maybe a double shift or a day when your schedule got mixed up. Describe what happened and explain why it stuck in your memory.

OK. Next, I'd like to ask your opinion. Some workers prefer flexible scheduling, where they can pick and swap their own shifts. Others prefer fixed shift times that stay the same every week. Which do you think works better, and why?

Good points. Let me ask you one final question. Some people think employers should be required to post shift schedules several weeks in advance, while others think that's unnecessary. Do you think employers should be required to do this? Explain your recommendation.

interview.topic: everyday routines and scheduling at a part-time workplace job
interview.premise: a workplace-culture researcher briefly interviews a person by phone about their part-time job routines, with no preparation time before each question
questionArc: Ask a concrete, retrievable fact about the kind of part-time workplace job the person has and the typical shift length or hours they work.
Ask the person to narrate one specific, memorable work shift experience, such as a double shift or a schedule mix-up, and explain why it stood out.
Present two contrasting views on flexible scheduling versus fixed shift times at a workplace and ask the person to take a side and justify it.
Broaden to a policy-level question about whether employers should be required to post shift schedules further in advance, inviting evaluation or a recommendation.
